topics.title: St Vincent: adult citizenship routes
topics.summary: Adult citizenship applications require route-specific eligibility and supporting evidence. The verified seven-year constitutional registration route concerns Commonwealth citizens; the complete ordinary naturalisation rules were not established from an accessible national statute in this collection.
topics.scope: Ordinary adult residence-based citizenship enquiry and the published application process; Commonwealth registration is identified separately, not presented as a universal naturalisation route.

facts.label: Seven years is a scoped registration rule
facts.text: Constitution section 93(2)(b) permits registration of Commonwealth citizens ordinarily resident for seven years immediately before application. Statutory refusal on defence, public-safety or public-order grounds remains possible; this is not the ordinary naturalisation rule for every nationality.
facts.locator: Constitution section 93(2)(b), its proviso and section 94

facts.label: Ordinary naturalisation clock unresolved
facts.text: The Prime Minister's FAQ mentions seven consecutive years of temporary residence or permanent-resident status for registration, without resolving the applicant cohorts. The full ordinary naturalisation clock, qualifying status and absence limits therefore remain unestablished here.
facts.locator: FAQ question 1; Constitution sections 93–94

facts.label: Identity, references and translations
facts.text: The citizenship checklist requests the application and reference page, certified photograph, birth certificate and passport biographical page, with spouse and marriage documents where applicable. Documents not in English require an official translation; originals are returned.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3, Citizenship section and final document note

facts.label: Medical and police evidence
facts.text: The checklist requires the applicant's medical certificate and a police certificate from the country most recently resided in for more than six months before arriving in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Additional applicable documents may be requested.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3, Citizenship items iv–v and additional-documents item vi

facts.label: Submission is not approval
facts.text: The office permits submission by mail, courier or a representative without being physically present when filing. Applications require investigation. Remote submission does not establish an exemption from the route's residence requirements or a guaranteed decision date.
facts.locator: FAQ questions 3–4

facts.label: Language and civic standard unresolved
facts.text: The collected official checklist and general guidance do not establish the ordinary route's language standard, testing procedure or exemptions. No CEFR level or exemption from testing is asserted.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3; citizenship guidance, application section

facts.label: Renunciation is a separate enquiry
facts.text: The office describes an application to renounce Vincentian citizenship, supported by the current passport and birth-certificate copy. That procedure does not establish whether an ordinary naturalisation applicant must renounce another nationality or can retain it; those questions remain unresolved here.
facts.locator: Citizenship guidance, Renunciation of Citizenship section

limits: The full current Citizenship Act was not obtained from an accessible national primary source. Constitutional Commonwealth registration and the office's general registration FAQ must not be flattened into a universal naturalisation clock.

The Constitution source is the government's copy marked updated in 2005. The citizenship checklist is undated; conflicting displayed fees are omitted. Descent, marriage and investment routes are outside this collection.

topics.title: St Vincent: personal income-tax scope
topics.summary: Personal tax depends on residence, ordinary residence and income source, not possession of a Vincentian passport. The law has multiple residence tests and a specific receipt-based foreign-income rule for limited resident cohorts.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income-tax residence, income scope and filing; no rates, tax calculation or comprehensive special-regime advice.

facts.label: Residence is not only a day count
facts.text: Residence includes a permanent abode with some presence, at least 183 days in the basis period, or presence continuous with qualifying presence in an adjoining year. The abode test preserves specified whole-year absences for education, medical treatment, government duties or government-sponsored labour schemes, subject to the Comptroller's satisfaction.
facts.locator: Section 2, resident definition (a)(i)–(iii), PDF page 12

facts.label: Resident and nonresident scope
facts.text: Residents generally include domestic and foreign income; nonresidents include Vincentian-source income. Ordinary residence specifically refers to the permanent-abode limb, not every resident. Employment exercised in the country is domestic-source regardless of where payment or the contract occurs.
facts.locator: Section 2, ordinarily resident; sections 8(1) and 10(1)(a)

facts.label: Limited foreign-income receipt rule
facts.text: Residents not ordinarily resident, and ordinarily resident officers or crew of international ships, include foreign income only to the extent received locally. Compulsory remittances under a government-contract overseas labour scheme are specifically included for ordinarily resident workers.
facts.locator: Section 8(2)–(3), PDF page 16

facts.label: Returns and withholding
facts.text: The revenue department lists 31 March after the calendar year as the personal income-tax return and payment deadline. Employer PAYE and withholding on covered payments to nonresidents are separate collection obligations; deductions do not turn citizenship into the tax-residence test.
facts.locator: Taxes page, Personal Income Tax, Pay As You Earn and Withholding Tax sections

facts.label: Agreement-specific double-tax relief
facts.text: Section 60 authorises double-taxation agreements, including source and relief rules, with agreements and changes published by Gazette order. Relief requires checking the applicable agreement; no universal exemption or particular treaty entitlement is established here.
facts.locator: Section 60(1)–(3), PDF page 53

limits: The IRD-hosted statutory compilation is not represented as a newly consolidated 2026 edition. Current guidance was read alongside it; rates, allowances and old subsidiary treaty lists are not reproduced as current entitlements.
General information only. Residence, source, remittance and agreement eligibility require individual analysis; corporate taxation and social contributions are outside this baseline.

topics.title: St Kitts and Nevis: adult naturalisation
topics.summary: Ordinary naturalisation is discretionary and distinct from Commonwealth registration or citizenship by investment. The posted statute requires a final residence year and separately refers to residence during the preceding fourteen years; its unusual wording is preserved rather than converted into a simple total.
topics.scope: Adult alien naturalisation under section 6 and Second Schedule paragraph 1; Commonwealth registration, British-protected-person alternatives, descent, marriage and investment are not interchangeable baseline routes.

facts.label: Final year and preceding-period wording
facts.text: An alien applicant must reside throughout the immediately preceding twelve months. The additional limb says the applicant has resided locally during the fourteen years preceding that year, without specifying an aggregate in that limb. Administrative interpretation of that wording remains unresolved; it is not labelled a simple fourteen-year total.
facts.locator: Second Schedule paragraph 1(a)–(b), printed page 15

facts.label: Absences and excluded residence
facts.text: Absences under six months and approved education, health or prescribed absences can count. Unlawful residence and custody outside a mental hospital do not; temporary immigration permission counts only with ministerial consent. Special circumstances can shift the final twelve-month period back by up to six months.
facts.locator: Section 2(7)–(8); Second Schedule paragraph 2

facts.label: Adult capacity, character and future home
facts.text: The applicant must be at least eighteen, of full capacity, of good character in the Minister's opinion and intend to reside locally after naturalisation.
facts.locator: Sections 2(3), 6; Second Schedule paragraph 1(c)–(d)

facts.label: Discretion, certificate and oath
facts.text: Meeting the qualifications does not compel a grant: the Minister retains discretion. Naturalisation uses Form N1; the oath or affirmation is required, normally within one calendar year of the certificate unless extended.
facts.locator: Section 6; Citizenship Regulations 4–6, printed page 17

facts.label: Language evidence unresolved
facts.text: No named language level, accepted evidence or test exemption was established from the collected ordinary-route provisions. This is not an assertion that no language assessment exists.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Second Schedule

facts.label: Dual-nationality protection is cohort-specific
facts.text: Constitution section 93 protects people entitled to registration under section 92 from refusal or compulsory renunciation solely because of another nationality. That express protection must not be extended to all ordinary naturalisation applicants; this collection does not settle their complete retention conditions.
facts.locator: Constitution sections 92–94, especially 93(1)–(2)

limits: The statutory source is the official 31 December 2020 revision. The separately read September 2026 descendant-registration bill is not treated as an operative ordinary-route amendment.

No single total residence number is asserted from the unusual Second Schedule wording. Commonwealth registration and British-protected-person rules differ. Language and ordinary-route foreign-nationality retention remain unresolved, not waived.

topics.title: St Kitts and Nevis: individual tax scope
topics.summary: The general income-tax charge ceased to apply to individuals in 1980, but this is not a tax-free-passport rule. Unincorporated business tax and withholding on covered payments to nonresidents require separate consideration.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income-tax charge, nonresident withholding and unincorporated business obligations; corporate residence rules are not substituted for personal rules.

facts.label: General individual income-tax charge removed
facts.text: Section 3(3) disapplies the general income-tax charge to income accruing from 1 May 1980 except income of a company liable under that section. The revenue department confirms abolition for individuals; this covers the general charge rather than eliminating every tax affecting a person.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 3(3), printed page 11; IRD corporate-income-tax page, opening historical explanation

facts.label: Do not revive old worldwide-income wording
facts.text: Section 3's domestic and foreign-income provisions must be read with the later individual exclusion. They are not a current general worldwide-income or remittance-basis charge on ordinary individuals. Separate business and withholding provisions can still matter.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 3(1)–(3), read together

facts.label: Covered payments to nonresidents
facts.text: Resident payers must withhold on covered income paid or credited to nonresidents, including specified interest, rent, fees, royalties and services. Section 36 expressly includes individuals; the payer can have this duty even when not otherwise an income-tax taxpayer.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 36(1), (4)–(8), printed pages 36–38

facts.label: Self-employment has a separate business tax
facts.text: Unincorporated business tax applies to covered business carried on locally, including personal services but excluding employment. Its ordinary base uses gross takings subject to statutory reductions, not net salary; qualifying businesses may instead make the Act's continuing election for Income Tax Act calculation.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2–5, especially 3 and 5(5)–(7)

facts.label: Quarterly business returns
facts.text: Persons liable for unincorporated business tax must file quarterly returns and pay by 15 March, June, September and December for the preceding quarter. Partners are jointly and severally liable, although one partner can be designated to file and pay.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 6–7; section 7 as substituted by Act 6 of 2014

facts.label: Residence and agreement limits
facts.text: No general individual 183-day tax-residence rule was established from these sources. The Income Tax Act allows double-taxation arrangements declared by order to override contrary enactments; any relief must match the relevant person, income and agreement.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act sections 3, 36(5) and 90

limits: The official tax statutes are revised to 31 December 2017. Current IRD confirmation of individual income-tax abolition was separately read. Rates and thresholds, which can be changed or temporarily reduced, are deliberately omitted.
A passport is not proof of tax residence or immunity from another country's tax. Social levies, contributions, VAT, property taxes and special business elections need separate advice.

topics.title: Antigua and Barbuda: adult naturalisation
topics.summary: Ordinary alien naturalisation combines a final residence year with five aggregate years in the preceding seven-year window. Good character, future residence and ministerial discretion remain separate requirements; Commonwealth registration and investment citizenship are different routes.
topics.scope: Adult alien naturalisation under section 6 and Second Schedule paragraph 1, read with the enacted 2021 residence-counting amendment; not descent, marriage, Commonwealth registration or investment citizenship.

facts.label: Final year plus five in the earlier seven
facts.text: The ordinary alien route requires twelve months' residence immediately before application and five aggregate years within the seven years preceding that final year. In special circumstances, the Minister can accept a final twelve-month period ending up to six months earlier.
facts.locator: Second Schedule paragraphs 1(a)–(b) and 2, PDF page 16

facts.label: Permitted absences and amended exclusions
facts.text: Short absences under six months and approved education, health or prescribed absences can count. The 2021 amendment excludes unlawful-residence periods totalling six months or more; it does not establish automatic credit for every shorter unlawful stay. Temporary permission requires ministerial consent to count; custody is excluded except mental-hospital detention.
facts.locator: Act section 2(7)–(8); Act 5 of 2021 section 2 replacing section 2(8)(a)

facts.label: Adult capacity, character and intention
facts.text: Applicants must be at least eighteen and of full capacity, satisfy the Minister as to good character, and intend to reside in Antigua and Barbuda if naturalised.
facts.locator: Sections 2(3), 6; Second Schedule paragraph 1(c)–(d)

facts.label: A discretionary grant and allegiance oath
facts.text: The Minister may grant a certificate after the statutory qualifications are satisfied. Citizenship follows the certificate and required allegiance oath; residence eligibility alone is not approval.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Third Schedule

facts.label: No inferred language exemption
facts.text: The collected naturalisation provisions do not establish a named language level, accepted test evidence or exemptions. Their silence is not a verified exemption from an interview or assessment.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Second Schedule

facts.label: Renunciation and dual-nationality scope
facts.text: Voluntary renunciation has a safeguard against remaining without another nationality. The Constitution's express dual-nationality protection concerns its specified independence-era citizens and registration cohort; ordinary naturalisation retention conditions are not fully established here.
facts.locator: Citizenship Act section 7; Constitution section 115(1)–(2), tied to 1 November 1981

limits: The government's base Act is read with Act 5 of 2021, published 13 May 2021; its older residence-exclusion wording must not be used alone. Commonwealth and British-protected-person routes have different residence rules.

The immigration FAQ could not be independently retrieved beyond search previews and is not cited. Language/testing and complete ordinary-route foreign-nationality retention conditions remain unresolved, not waived.

topics.title: Antigua and Barbuda: individual tax scope
topics.summary: Personal income tax was abolished in 2016, but unincorporated business income, including covered rents, remains a separate tax concern. Its legislation distinguishes employment, local business connections, foreign-source conditions and nonresident collection duties.
topics.scope: Baseline individual employment and unincorporated-business income treatment, incorporated residence definition, foreign-income qualifications and nonresident obligations; not company taxation or a tax calculation.

facts.label: Abolition does not exempt all personal income
facts.text: The IRD confirms personal income-tax abolition followed by unincorporated business tax from 1 July 2016. Self-employment, sole traders, partnerships and covered rents fall within that separate regime; employment income is excluded.
facts.locator: IRD FAQ questions 1–4; Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2 and 4(2)(e)

facts.label: Several individual residence tests
facts.text: The business-tax law adopts the Income Tax Act's residence definition: permanent abode plus some presence, at least 183 days in the basis period, or presence continuous with qualifying presence in an adjoining year. The abode limb preserves specified whole-year education, medical or government-duty absences subject to the Commissioner's satisfaction.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act section 2; Income Tax Act section 2, resident definition (a)(i)–(iii), printed pages 6–7

facts.label: Foreign business income is conditional
facts.text: The business-tax charge can cover income arising abroad whether remitted or not. Its foreign-source exemption requires both no incidental connection to activity in Antigua and Barbuda and liability to tax in the source jurisdiction. Separate relief concerns temporary visitors without resident intent and under six months' actual residence in the income year.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2, 3, 4(2)(d), 4(3) and 10(d)(i); printed pages 7–12

facts.label: Nonresident property and withholding
facts.text: Nonresident rental-property owners must appoint a property-management agent for tax and filing duties. Payments to nonresident individuals can attract withholding for specified rent, interest and other chargeable income; nonresidence is not a blanket exemption.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 16–17; IRD FAQ questions 9–10

facts.label: Returns and agreement-specific exemptions
facts.text: Covered businesses file quarterly and an annual return by 31 March after the year-end. The Act also recognises income exemptions under applicable government agreements; agreement coverage and conditions must be checked rather than assuming automatic foreign-tax relief.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 4(2)(c), 12–13; IRD FAQ question 7

limits: The current official collection uses the 2016 business-tax Act and posted IRD FAQ; the 2019 registration amendment was also read and does not supply a new residence test. The older Income Tax Act is used only for the definition expressly incorporated by the business-tax statute.

No generic territorial-tax or tax-free-passport label is justified. General information only: particular income classification, other-country taxation, treaty access and social contributions require separate analysis. Rates and monetary thresholds are omitted.
